slides.title: Grow instead of search?
slides.subtitle: Function-preserving depth growth as a cheap alternative to depth search for multi-task PPO on Meta-World MT10
slides.footer: COMP9501 Advanced Machine Learning  ·  exploratory study  ·  43 training runs, 5 seeds
slides.notes: Today we ask a practical question about reinforcement-learning policies: if you do not know how deep your policy network should be, can you grow it during a single training run instead of training several networks and picking the best one?

slides.title: Choosing network depth usually means training K networks
bullets: Depth is a hyperparameter: too shallow underfits, too deep may waste compute
Standard answer is **search**: train one network per candidate depth, keep the best on validation
- Cost grows linearly with the number of candidates K
In RL each run is expensive: millions of simulator steps
**Growth**: start shallow, insert layers during one run, pay for one run
slides.takeaway: Question: can one growing run match a searched depth at lower total cost?
slides.notes: The default way to deal with an unknown architecture hyperparameter is search. You train one network per depth and keep the one that does best on validation data. This multiplies the training cost by the number of candidates. In reinforcement learning every run is millions of simulator steps, so that is expensive. Growth is the alternative: start with a shallow network and add layers as training goes.

slides.title: What we set out to test
cards: Can a layer be added safely?
Insert a layer mid-training without breaking the learned policy
Checked at every insertion and in the learning curves afterwards
Does depth matter here?
If all depths perform the same, search is unnecessary and growth is pointless
Measured by a full sweep over depth 1–4
Is growth cheaper than search?
Compare one growing run against grid search, successive halving, default and random depth
Cost in environment steps and learner FLOPs
slides.takeaway: Problem framing: no known good depth in advance, and compute counts the search too
slides.notes: We broke the question into three parts. First, can we add a layer without destroying what the policy has already learned? Second, does depth actually matter on this benchmark, because if it does not, there is nothing to search for. Third, if it matters, is one growing run cheaper than searching, once we count the cost of the search itself.

slides.title: Identity insertion: a new layer that changes nothing at first
bullets: Existing weights and their Adam state are kept; the new layer starts fresh; the critic is untouched
Checked at all **20** insertions in our runs: zero change to the policy
slides.takeaway: Identity insertion adds capacity without an insertion shock
slides.notes: We append a square linear layer initialised to the identity, followed by a ReLU, between the last hidden layer and the policy head. Its input already comes out of a ReLU and is non-negative, so the identity followed by a ReLU returns it unchanged: the policy is exactly the same at the moment of insertion. Existing weights keep their Adam state, the new layer starts with fresh optimiser state, and the critic is not changed. Our code asserts this at every insertion.

slides.title: Ten robot tasks, goal positions held out from training
rows: Meta-World MT10, 10 manipulation tasks, one policy
50 variants per task: 30 train / 10 validation / 10 test
8× A6000 server, Modal T4s, RTX 4070, RTX 3050
bullets: Only the actor depth or growth schedule changes between runs
Model selection uses validation goals; all reported numbers are held-out test goals
slides.takeaway: Same recipe, same budget: only depth and its timing vary
slides.notes: Everything is held fixed except the actor depth or the growth schedule. Each task has fifty goal variants; we train on thirty, select models on ten and report on the remaining ten. Every run gets three million environment steps and is evaluated every five hundred thousand steps on train, validation and test goals.

slides.title: What growth competes against, and how cost is counted
cards: Search baselines
**Grid search**: train depth 1–4 fully, pick best on validation: 12M steps
**Successive halving**: all 4 depths to 0.5M, best 2 to 1.5M, best 1 to 3M: 5.5M steps
Simulated on the logged learning curves of the same runs
No-search baselines
**Default depth 2**: the recipe's usual choice
**Random depth**: average over depth 1–4, the expected result of guessing
**Best depth in hindsight**: an upper reference, not achievable without search
Growth schedules
Start at depth 1, insert to depth 3
**Grow early**: at 0.5M and 1M steps
**Grow late**: at 1M and 2M steps
One run, 3M steps
slides.takeaway: Cost = learner FLOPs (and environment steps) spent before a final model is chosen
slides.notes: We compare against two families. Search methods pay for several runs: grid search pays for four full runs; successive halving starts all four depths, cuts half at five hundred thousand steps and keeps one from one and a half million, total 5.5 million steps. We simulate it from the logged curves, so no extra training. No-search methods pay for one run but must commit to a depth: the default depth two, or a random guess. Best depth in hindsight is an upper reference.

slides.title: Held-out goals are not harder than training goals
bullets: Train and held-out success differ by at most ~4 points for every configuration
Goal variants interpolate object and target positions within each task
slides.takeaway: The held-out split is a sound test, but it does not make MT10 harder
slides.notes: One motivation for this setup was that earlier experiments only looked at training-goal success and reached above ninety percent. With held-out goals we see the same numbers within a few points. The goal variants within a task interpolate each other, so the split does not make the benchmark harder. What does make a difference is depth.

slides.title: Depth matters, mainly on the harder tasks
bullets: Mean held-out success: depth 1 **64%** → depth 2 **81%** → depth 3 **84%** → depth 4 **88%**
Gains come from **peg-insert-side** (0 → 76%), **push** (22 → 88%) and **drawer-open** (40 → 100%)
slides.takeaway: The wrong depth costs up to 24 points, so choosing it is worth paying for
slides.notes: Depth matters on this benchmark: mean held-out success rises from 64 percent with one hidden layer to 88 percent with four. Per task, six tasks are solved at every depth; the gains come from peg insertion, pushing and drawer opening. The best depth is three for two seeds and four for three.

slides.title: Growing runs never dip, they just need time at full depth
bullets: No drop at any insertion: every growth event had max output error 0
Each insert adds 160k actor parameters (21k → 182k → 342k)
Early growth leaves 2M steps at depth 3 and catches up
Late growth leaves only 1M steps and ends near depth 2
slides.takeaway: When to grow matters more than whether to grow
slides.notes: Here are the individual seeds. Dotted lines mark the insertions. Success never drops at an insertion, consistent with the identity property. What differs is how long the network gets at its final depth: early growth has two million steps at depth three and catches up with the fixed deep networks; late growth has one million and finishes near depth two.

slides.title: At equal compute, a growing run is well ahead of search
stats: successive halving at the same spend
compute search needs to catch up
slides.takeaway: Search only overtakes growth after spending about twice the compute
slides.notes: Here the x-axis is total learner compute spent so far, including every run a search keeps alive, and the y-axis is the held-out success of the model the strategy would pick at that point using validation goals. A growing run spends its compute on a single network, so after 0.18 petaFLOP it is at 84 percent, while successive halving at the same spend is still around 60 percent and grid search lower. Successive halving needs about 0.33 petaFLOP to pass growth, and grid search reaches 89 percent only at 0.71.

slides.title: Grow early matches successive halving at half its compute
bullets: Grid search: **89%** for 0.71 PFLOP (4 runs, 12M steps)
Successive halving: **85%** for 0.36 PFLOP (5.5M steps)
Grow early: **84%** for 0.18 PFLOP (1 run, 3M steps)
Beats default depth 2 (81%) and a random depth (79%)
Still **5 points** below the best fixed depth
slides.takeaway: One growing run ≈ cheap search at half the compute, but not yet as good as a full search
slides.notes: Main result, paired by seed, with cost measured in learner FLOPs. Grid search finds the best depth, 89 percent, for 0.71 petaFLOP across four runs. Successive halving reaches 85 percent for 0.36. Growing early reaches 84 percent for 0.18, about half the compute of successive halving and a quarter of grid search, and better than committing to the default or a random depth. It is still 5 points below the best fixed depth. In environment steps the picture is the same: 3M for growing versus 5.5M and 12M.

slides.title: Growth spends its early training in a small network
bullets: Cost standard: **learner FLOPs** of actor + critic
- 2P per sample for rollouts, 16 × 6P for PPO epochs
Depth 4 costs **2.3×** depth 1 per run
Grow early: **0.18 PFLOP**, less than one depth-3 (0.20) or depth-4 (0.25) run
Hardware-independent, unlike wall-clock time
slides.takeaway: Measured in FLOPs, a growing run is cheaper than training the final depth from the start
slides.notes: We use learner FLOPs as the cost standard: forward passes during rollouts plus forward and backward passes during the sixteen PPO epochs, for actor and critic. Deeper actors cost more per run. Growing early spends its first million steps in one- and two-layer networks, so a whole growing run costs less than training depth three or four from scratch. FLOPs do not depend on which GPU a run used, so runs on different hardware are comparable.

slides.title: With a narrow actor (width 128), growth does not help
bullets: Best fixed depth: **82%**; successive halving: **80%**
Grow early: **71%**; grow late: **66%**
Both are below a random depth (72%)
Only 2 seeds, so a warning sign rather than a conclusion
slides.takeaway: Growth is not a free lunch: its benefit depends on width and schedule
slides.notes: We repeated the study with a narrow actor. Here growth did not help at all and ended below a random depth. We only have two seeds, so we treat this as a warning sign. It suggests the benefit of growth depends on width and on the schedule.

slides.title: What this study does not show
cards: Scope
One benchmark (MT10), one algorithm (PPO)
5 seeds at width 400, 2 at width 128
3M-step budget; longer runs could change the ranking
Method
Fixed growth schedules, not an adaptive trigger
Successive halving is simulated from logged curves
Not the full grow–keep–prune controller
Measurement
Held-out goals are interpolations, not new tasks
Cost counts learner FLOPs and steps, not wall-clock time
100 held-out episodes per evaluation: about ±4 points per run
slides.takeaway: Treat the result as evidence for early growth, not a validated method
slides.notes: Several limitations. It is one benchmark with five seeds. The growth schedule is fixed by hand rather than triggered by a plateau. Successive halving is simulated from the same curves. And held-out goals test interpolation, not new tasks.

slides.title: Takeaways and next steps
points: Identity insertion grows a policy safely
Zero change at all 20 insertions, no success dip afterwards
64% → 88% from depth 1 to 4; held-out goals add no difficulty
Grow early ≈ successive halving at half the compute
84% vs 85%, but 5 points below the best depth; no gain at width 128
Plateau-triggered growth, growing beyond depth 3, more seeds, MT50
slides.notes: To summarise: identity insertion lets a policy grow without breaking it; depth matters on this benchmark; and growing early gives search-level performance for the price of one run, though not best-depth performance. The natural next step is to decide when to grow adaptively, for example when learning plateaus.
